title: AI powered entomology: Lessons from millions of AI code reviews — Tomas Reimers, Graphite

summary: Tomas Reimers, co-founder of Graphite, introduces Diamond, an AI-powered code reviewer that connects to GitHub and finds bugs. The project started roughly a year ago when Graphite noticed AI-generated code was increasing bug counts. Early experiments with Claude yielded impressive bug discoveries—e.g., returning uninstantiated database ORM classes, or division by negative numbers in border-radius math—but also frustrating false positives like incorrect CSS suggestions or requests to revert working code. Graphite realized LLMs produce multiple types of comments, not all useful or welcome. A key insight came when designers struggled to understand why developers accepted some LLM comments but rejected others that looked similar: developers tolerate pedantic comments from humans but find them annoying from LLMs. This led to a two-axis classification: whether the LLM can catch the issue, and whether humans want to receive that comment from an LLM. Graphite analyzed 10,000 comments from their own and open-source codebases, categorizing them into bugs, accidentally committed code, performance/security concerns, documentation mismatches, stylistic changes, tribal knowledge, and code cleanliness/best practices. The desirable quadrant—LLM can catch and humans want—became the target. Measuring success involved two metrics: downvote rate (currently under 4%) and action rate, the percentage of comments leading to code changes. Human comments lead to action roughly 50% of the time; Diamond reached 52% by March, suggesting properly prompted AI review can match human fidelity.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Graphite's product Diamond is an AI code reviewer connected to GitHub, launched about a year ago to address rising bugs in AI-generated code.
Early experiments with Claude found real bugs but also produced frustrating false positives, motivating a deeper classification of comment types.
Graphite discovered a two-axis framework: what LLMs can/cannot catch, and what humans do/do not want to receive from an LLM.

Analysis of 10,000 comments from own and open-source codebases revealed categories including bugs, accidentally committed code, performance/security, documentation, stylistic changes, tribal knowledge, and code cleanliness.
Code cleanliness and best-practice comments are technically correct but often unwelcome from LLMs, while tribal knowledge comments are wanted but hard for LLMs to produce.
Graphite prompts the LLM to operate only in the desirable quadrant—comments it can catch and humans want to receive.
Success is measured via downvote rate (under 4%) and action rate—percentage of comments leading to actual code changes.
About 50% of human code review comments lead to changes within the same PR; Diamond reached 52% by March.
The broader thesis is that AI code review genuinely works when LLMs are correctly prompted and scoped.
As context and model capabilities grow, the boundaries of the desirable quadrant may shift, requiring continuous re-measurement.

sections.title: Introduction to Graphite and Diamond
sections.summary: Tomas Reimers introduces himself as co-founder of Graphite, which builds Diamond, an AI-powered code reviewer connected to GitHub. The project began about a year ago as AI-generated code and bug counts both rose.

sections.title: Early AI bug-finding experiments
sections.summary: Graphite experimented with Claude on PRs and found impressive early results, including real bugs like uninstantiated ORM classes causing server crashes and border-radius math causing division by negative numbers. However, these experiments also yielded frustrating false positives.

sections.title: Frustrating LLM experiences and classification insight
sections.summary: LLMs also produced unhelpful comments like incorrect CSS suggestions or requests to revert working code. Graphite began categorizing comments and noticed that developers had consistent opinions about which comments were acceptable from LLMs versus humans, while designers found this distinction baffling.

sections.title: Two-axis framework and designer feedback
sections.summary: A pivotal moment came when designers couldn't understand why developers accepted some LLM comments but rejected seemingly similar ones. Graphite realized there are two axes: what LLMs can catch and what humans want to receive from an LLM. Pedantic comments may be tolerable from humans but annoying from LLMs.

sections.title: 10,000 comment analysis and bug taxonomy
sections.summary: Graphite fed 10,000 comments from their own and open-source codebases to LLMs for categorization. They identified bug types including logical bugs, accidentally committed code, performance/security concerns, documentation mismatches, stylistic changes, tribal knowledge, and code cleanliness/best practices. The top-right quadrant—LLM can catch and humans want—became the operational target.

sections.title: Measuring success: downvotes and action rate
sections.summary: Graphite added upvote/downvote reactions to detect hallucinations, achieving under 4% downvote rate. They then measured action rate: the percentage of comments leading to actual code changes, finding roughly 50% of human comments lead to action within the PR.

sections.title: Results and closing thesis
sections.summary: Diamond reached a 52% action rate by March, matching human-level fidelity. Reimers concludes that AI code review works when LLMs are properly prompted and scoped, and invites attendees to try Diamond at their booth.
